questions.question: What compromise does Henry make with York in Parliament?

options.text: Henry keeps the crown for life, but York and his heirs will succeed him.
York gives up his claim in exchange for the throne of France.
Henry’s son succeeds at once while York becomes his guardian.
Warwick becomes king until Henry’s son comes of age.

questions.explanation: Henry disinherits his son and entails the crown on York’s line in return for an end to war during his own life.

evidence.exact:
KING HENRY.
Not for myself, Lord Warwick, but my son,
Whom I unnaturally shall disinherit.
But be it as it may, [To York.] I here entail
The crown to thee and to thine heirs for ever;
Conditionally, that here thou take an oath
To cease this civil war, and whilst I live,
To honour me as thy king and sovereign,
And neither by treason nor hostility
To seek to put me down and reign thyself.

questions.question: How does Richard argue that York can break his promise to let Henry reign?

options.text: He claims Parliament has already released York from the oath.
He claims the oath is void because Henry lacks lawful authority.
He says Margaret has accepted York as the reigning king.
He says Warwick took the oath in York’s place.

questions.explanation: Richard treats Henry as a usurper and therefore denies that the oath binds York.

evidence.exact:
RICHARD.
An oath is of no moment, being not took
Before a true and lawful magistrate
That hath authority over him that swears.
Henry had none, but did usurp the place;
Then, seeing ’twas he that made you to depose,
Your oath, my lord, is vain and frivolous.
Therefore, to arms! And, father, do but think
How sweet a thing it is to wear a crown,
Within whose circuit is Elysium
And all that poets feign of bliss and joy.
Why do we linger thus? I cannot rest
Until the white rose that I wear be dyed
Even in the lukewarm blood of Henry’s heart.

YORK.
Richard, enough; I will be king, or die.

She makes him carry Henry’s royal train.
She places a paper crown on his head.
She orders him to marry Lady Bona.

questions.explanation: The paper crown turns York’s claim to kingship into a public humiliation.

questions.question: What does the son’s discovery on the battlefield show about the civil war?

options.text: It has united all families under Warwick’s command.
It has kept ordinary people safely outside the conflict.
It has ended the rivalry between Henry and York.
It has forced close relatives onto opposing sides and made a son kill his father unknowingly.

questions.explanation: The son says he and his father were pressed into opposing armies and that he did not recognize his father before killing him.

evidence.exact:
SON.
Ill blows the wind that profits nobody.
This man, whom hand to hand I slew in fight,
May be possessed with some store of crowns;
And I, that haply take them from him now,
May yet ere night yield both my life and them
To some man else, as this dead man doth me.
Who’s this? O God! It is my father’s face,
Whom in this conflict I unwares have killed.
O heavy times, begetting such events!
From London by the King was I pressed forth;
My father, being the Earl of Warwick’s man,
Came on the part of York, pressed by his master;
And I, who at his hands received my life,
Have by my hands of life bereaved him.
Pardon me, God, I knew not what I did;
And pardon, father, for I knew not thee.
My tears shall wipe away these bloody marks,
And no more words till they have flowed their fill.
evidence.prefix: er, bringing in the dead body.

questions.question: What boundary does Lady Grey insist on during Edward’s courtship?

options.text: She will not become his concubine, though he speaks of love.
She will accept him only if he first crowns Warwick.
She will marry him only after joining Margaret’s army.
She will abandon her children’s claim to their lands for a place at court.

questions.explanation: Lady Grey distinguishes the honorable position of queen from a sexual relationship without marriage.

evidence.exact:
LADY GREY.
And that is more than I will yield unto.
I know I am too mean to be your queen,
And yet too good to be your concubine.
evidence.prefix: is to enjoy thee for my love.

questions.question: Why does Warwick transfer his allegiance from Edward to Henry?

options.text: Henry gives Warwick the crown for the rest of his life.
Edward’s marriage to Lady Grey humiliates his embassy to arrange a match with Bona.
Margaret admits that she forged Edward’s marriage contract.
Richard persuades Warwick that Edward has died in captivity.

questions.explanation: Warwick regards Edward’s secret marriage as a dishonor to himself and Bona and vows to restore Henry.

evidence.exact:
KING LEWIS.
What, has your king married the Lady Grey,
And now, to soothe your forgery and his,
Sends me a paper to persuade me patience?
Is this th’ alliance that he seeks with France?
Dare he presume to scorn us in this manner?
evidence.suffix:
QUEEN MARGARET.
I told your ma

evidence.exact:
WARWICK.
King Lewis, I here protest in sight of heaven,
And by the hope I have of heavenly bliss,
That I am clear from this misdeed of Edward’s—
No more my king, for he dishonours me,
But most himself, if he could see his shame.
Did I forget that by the house of York
My father came untimely to his death?
Did I let pass th’ abuse done to my niece?
Did I impale him with the regal crown?
Did I put Henry from his native right?
And am I guerdoned at the last with shame?
Shame on himself, for my desert is honour;
And to repair my honour lost for him,
I here renounce him and return to Henry.
My noble Queen, let former grudges pass,
And henceforth I am thy true servitor.
I will revenge his wrong to Lady Bona,
And replant Henry in his former state.

questions.question: How is the captive Edward enabled to escape?

options.text: Margaret releases him after he promises to support her son.
Warwick sends him to France as an ambassador to Bona.
His allies meet him with horses and men during a lightly guarded hunting outing.
The Tower’s lieutenant frees him when Henry abdicates.

questions.explanation: Richard uses Edward’s freedom to hunt as cover for a planned rescue.

evidence.exact:
RICHARD.
Now, my Lord Hastings and Sir William Stanley,
Leave off to wonder why I drew you hither
Into this chiefest thicket of the park.
Thus stands the case: you know our King, my brother,
Is prisoner to the Bishop here, at whose hands
He hath good usage and great liberty,
And often but attended with weak guard,
Comes hunting this way to disport himself.
I have advertised him by secret means
That if about this hour he make this way,
Under the colour of his usual game,
He shall here find his friends with horse and men
To set him free from his captivity.

questions.question: Why does Clarence abandon Warwick and return to Edward before the battle?

options.text: He learns that Warwick plans to marry Lady Grey.
He believes Margaret has named him heir to France.
He wants to restore the original bargain between Henry and York.
He refuses to destroy his own family by fighting his brother.

questions.explanation: Clarence casts off Warwick’s badge and calls war against his brother unnatural.

evidence.exact:
Look here, I throw my infamy at thee.
I will not ruinate my father’s house,
Who gave his blood to lime the stones together,
And set up Lancaster. Why, trowest thou, Warwick,
That Clarence is so harsh, so blunt, unnatural,
To bend the fatal instruments of war
Against his brother and his lawful King?
Perhaps thou wilt object my holy oath.
To keep that oath were more impiety
Than Jephthah’s when he sacrificed his daughter.
I am so sorry for my trespass made
That, to deserve well at my brother’s hands,
I here proclaim myself thy mortal foe,
With resolution, whereso’er I meet thee—
As I will meet thee if thou stir abroad—
To plague thee for thy foul misleading me.
And so, proud-hearted Warwick, I defy thee,
And to my brother turn my blushing cheeks.
Pardon me, Edward, I will make amends.
And, Richard, do not frown upon my faults,
For I will henceforth be no more unconstant.

questions.question: What happens to Margaret’s son after his capture at Tewkesbury?

options.text: Edward, Richard, and Clarence stab him after he defies them.
He is exchanged for Warwick and returned to France.
He is crowned king under Clarence’s guardianship.
He escapes with Henry to the Tower of London.

questions.explanation: The captive prince asserts his family’s right, and the three brothers answer by stabbing him.

evidence.exact:
PRINCE EDWARD.
I know my duty; you are all undutiful.
Lascivious Edward, and thou perjured George,
And thou misshapen Dick, I tell ye all
I am your better, traitors as ye are,
And thou usurp’st my father’s right and mine.

KING EDWARD.
Take that, the likeness of this railer here.

[Stabs him.]

RICHARD.
Sprawl’st thou? Take that to end thy agony.

[Stabs him.]

GEORGE.
And there’s for twitting me with perjury.

[Stabs him.]

QUEEN MARGARET.
O, kill me too!

questions.question: What does Richard do to Henry in the Tower?

options.text: He frees Henry to challenge Edward again.
He kills Henry after cutting off his prophetic denunciation.
He crowns Henry in return for being named heir.
He takes Henry to France to join Margaret.

questions.explanation: Richard interrupts Henry’s warnings with a stab and then strikes his body again.

evidence.exact:
RICHARD.
I’ll hear no more. Die, prophet, in thy speech.

[Stabs him.]

For this, amongst the rest, was I ordained.

KING HENRY.
Ay, and for much more slaughter after this.
O God, forgive my sins, and pardon thee!

[Dies.]

RICHARD.
What, will the aspiring blood of Lancaster
Sink in the ground? I thought it would have mounted.
See how my sword weeps for the poor King’s death.
O, may such purple tears be always shed
From those that wish the downfall of our house!
If any spark of life be yet remaining,
Down, down to hell; and say I sent thee thither—

[Stabs him again.]
